title: Personal Financial Management Practices and Their Influence on Saving Behavior Among Bureau of the Treasury Personnel
tldr: A mixed-methods study of 327 Bureau of the Treasury employees finds that budgeting is the most practiced PFM behavior while saving is least practiced, with budgeting showing the strongest positive influence on saving behavior and emergency funds being the top savings objective.
problem_and_motivation: Despite the Bureau of the Treasury's role in financial management, its employees face personal finance challenges mirroring broader population issues. There is limited research on the financial practices of government finance professionals in the Philippines, particularly those in treasury roles who should theoretically demonstrate strong financial management. Understanding their practices can provide insights applicable to broader Filipino financial wellness.
approach: Administered structured self-administered questionnaires to 327 employees across all BTr branches nationwide.
Conducted semi-structured interviews with 15 participants selected through purposive and snowball sampling.
Analyzed demographic profiles using frequency counts and percentages.
Computed mean scores and standard deviations for PFM practice items across budgeting, saving, investing, debt management, and financial planning.
Performed Pearson correlation analysis to examine relationships between PFM practices and saving behavior.
Applied multiple regression analysis to determine influence of PFM practices on saving behavior.
Conducted thematic analysis of qualitative responses using the six-phase Braun and Clarke framework.
Tested reliability using Cronbach's Alpha (0.820) indicating acceptable internal consistency.
findings: Budgeting is the most practiced PFM component; saving is the least practiced.
Budgeting has the strongest positive influence on saving behavior among BTr employees.
Emergency fund creation is the primary savings objective.
Multiple revenue streams do not necessarily translate to higher savings rates.
Younger employees under 30 demonstrate more disciplined financial practices than older colleagues.
Single employees exhibit stronger saving habits than married counterparts.
Informal budgeting approaches persist even among finance professionals.
Employees maintain personal finances separately from their professional roles at BTr.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This mixed-methods study provides the first comprehensive analysis of PFM practices among Philippine government finance professionals, demonstrating that even those in treasury roles exhibit budgeting and saving behavior patterns similar to the general population. It establishes budgeting as the strongest predictor of saving behavior, identifies demographic differences in financial practices (younger employees more disciplined), and reveals that emergency fund creation is the primary savings objective, offering actionable insights for organizational financial wellness programs.
directly_justifies: Budgeting is the most practiced PFM component and strongest predictor of saving behavior.
Saving is the least practiced PFM component despite respondents being finance professionals.
Emergency fund creation is the primary savings objective across all demographics.
Younger employees under 30 demonstrate more disciplined financial practices.
Multiple revenue streams do not necessarily translate to higher savings rates.
limits: Cross-sectional design prevents causal inference about PFM practice influences.
Self-reported data may introduce social desirability bias among finance professionals.
Single-organization study (BTr) limits generalizability to other populations.
Convenience sampling approach may not represent all government employees.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: The paper was systematically scanned across all 14 topic domains. Domain 5 (Behavioral Profiles) received high relevance as the core study profiles financial behaviors among government employees. Domain 7 (Budgeting) received high relevance for its analysis of budgeting as strongest predictor. Domain 4 (Existing Systems) received medium relevance for contextualizing PFM practices. Domains 1, 2, 3, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11, 13, and 14 were considered and rejected as the paper does not focus on Filipino demographics beyond BTr employees, financial data APIs, expense categorization, predictive modeling, anomaly detection, mobile design, or synthetic data generation.

limitations: Self-report bias may inflate reported positive financial behaviors.
Convenience sampling may not represent broader government employee population.
